findings.reason: The protected Python solution sorts all grid cells (val, row, col) by value, and iterates through them maintaining row_max and col_max arrays. For each cell, score = max(row_max[r], col_max[c]) + 1, which is assigned to answer[r][c] and updates row_max[r] and col_max[c]. The greedy sorting solution runs in O(N log N) time and O(N) space; no candidate is required.

Since original grid values are distinct, sorting guarantees that all smaller elements in a cell's row and column are processed first. Assigning max(row_max[r], col_max[c]) + 1 gives each cell the minimal possible value that preserves row/column relative order.

Sorting N = m * n cell triples takes O(N log N) time. Updating row and column maxima takes O(N) time. Total time complexity is O(N log N) with O(N) auxiliary space for sorted cells and output matrix. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts m x n matrix grid, preserves row and column relative order, and returns a new m x n matrix minimizing the overall maximum value.

The approach accurately details sorting cell dependencies, tracking row_max and col_max arrays, greedy minimum score assignment, and O(N log N) time / O(N) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover DAG topological sorting, repeated minimum search, single row/column matrices, unrelated cells, single cell matrices, and distinct original values.
